title: Property insurance for a school or kindergarten
excerpt: How a school or kindergarten in Moldova can prepare an insurance assessment: premises, equipment, activities and responsibilities. Property, personal accidents and liability require separate checks.
imageAlt: School administrators checking furniture and equipment in a modern empty classroom without children present

seo.title: School and kindergarten property insurance in Moldova | ING Broker
seo.description: Prepare inventory, ownership, premises and activities. Do not confuse property protection with children's medical insurance or institutional liability.
seo.keywords: school insurance Moldova, kindergarten property insurance, educational equipment insurance, school liability assessment, classroom inventory

author: ING Broker editorial team
content:
For a school or kindergarten, an insurance assessment starts with the institution's property, activities and responsibilities. The building, furniture, computers and kitchen equipment should not automatically be treated as one insured subject. Insurance for property does not confirm payment for a child's accident or protection against every claim made by a parent or visitor.

This article helps administrators in the Republic of Moldova prepare for an assessment. It does not announce a special package available to every institution or establish a legal obligation to buy insurance. A local example of property insurance for legal entities illustrates a product category. Whether an educational institution can be accepted, and on what terms, must be confirmed separately.

Who uses the building and who owns the property?

Establish whether the institution owns the premises, rents them or uses them under another contractual arrangement. Prepare the relevant documents and distinguish improvements made by the institution from a building owned by someone else. A landlord's policy does not prove that all the school's equipment is protected. Paying for routine repairs does not, by itself, identify the interest that can be considered for insurance.

Use the existing documents to identify responsibility for maintenance, installations and shared areas. Explain any division of the building between different operators. Do not tell parents that the building is insured for every situation on the strength of a document covering another party, selected rooms or a limited category of property.

Prepare the inventory by room and category

Organise the list around classrooms, administrative rooms, kitchens, storage areas and other spaces actually used. Record furniture, equipment and assets with values supported by available documents. Include identifiers for important devices, without publishing a detailed security inventory online. An organised list supports comparison and later documentation, but does not replace the description required by the insurer for its assessment.

Separate the institution's property from personal items belonging to children, employees or service providers. A computer temporarily brought in by a teacher, or a borrowed musical instrument, may have a different owner and contractual status. Ask expressly about these situations. Do not promise protection for personal possessions in public communications without documented confirmation of the applicable conditions and limits.

Describe the activities as they actually operate

Explain the type of institution, its opening hours and the activities carried out on the premises. Identify workshops, clubs, meals, sports or events separately where relevant. A general description such as office does not accurately describe a building used for daily activities with children. Accurate information is needed for the discussion, but does not mean that every activity will be accepted.

If rooms are hired out in the evenings for other purposes, include that arrangement in the assessment. Also explain the relationship with other operators working at the same address. Do not infer protection for them from the main institution's name. Their roles and conditions require separate checks; a service provider's responsibility does not automatically transfer simply because an event takes place inside the building.

Ask specific questions about fire, water and installations

For property, request the list of causes considered and the product's definitions. Ask what would need to be checked after an electrical incident or a water leak in a computer room. These are preparation questions, not a list of risks guaranteed to be included. Each proposal should explain what is accepted, excluded or subject to particular conditions.

Prepare the maintenance records and inspection information that actually exist. Do not invent confirmation that the building is compliant. Mark any missing technical document and ask for clarification. Insurance does not replace safety responsibilities, maintenance or specialist intervention. This article cannot certify the condition of installations and must not be used to justify delaying action on a known hazard.

The institution's liability requires a separate assessment

Insurance for a building concerns the property described, subject to the accepted terms. A claim made against the institution by another person raises different questions about responsibility, the alleged act and the loss. Do not assume that a furniture policy resolves such claims. Ask for the actual activities, relevant people and circumstances to be examined when considering a possible separate solution.

Not every accident automatically establishes the institution's liability, and not every demand creates an obligation for the insurer to pay. This article provides no legal conclusion for an individual case. If an incident occurs, protecting people, informing the competent contacts and recording the facts accurately take priority. Obtain specialist assistance to assess responsibility and the steps required in the actual circumstances.

Personal accidents are not the same as property damage

If the administrator wants protection for people to be considered, make a separate request. Accident insurance, civil liability and property insurance have different subjects. Do not describe property insurance to parents as medical protection for children. The availability of a product for a group, and its conditions, must be confirmed separately before any commercial announcement.

Do not collect children's medical information through a public form for an initial comparison. The first discussion can use aggregated information about activities and objectives. Any necessary documents can then be requested through an appropriate channel. Information requirements and personal-data rules need their own review. This material does not establish a legal basis for processing children's records.

Check the kitchen and services supplied by other businesses

Where meals are provided, describe the space, equipment and operator. Distinguish the institution's assets from equipment brought in by the service provider. Check the cooperation documents to establish who maintains appliances and what information is relevant to the assessment. Mentioning a kitchen does not confirm protection for every food item, incident or loss associated with the service.

Apply the same approach to security, cleaning, transport and activities organised by third parties. Prepare the relevant contracts when requested. Do not assume that a provider's insurance automatically includes the institution. If a document is presented as evidence, read the insured party, activity, period and limits. Possessing a policy copy does not explain the entire relationship between the parties.

Grounds, outdoor facilities and trips need distinct checks

Describe the outdoor areas used by the institution and the property kept there. Ask whether they appear in the proposal and how they are treated. Do not extend an offer for a particular building to every place where the institution operates merely by assumption. The addresses, uses and property should be recognisable in the documents.

Excursions, journeys and activities at other locations merit separate questions about the organiser and responsibilities. Premises insurance does not establish protection for a coach, its passengers or property in transit. This distinction does not announce a universal solution. It identifies where further assessment is needed before communicating any specific protection to parents.

Compare values, deductibles and interruption costs

Support the declared values with available documents and ask which valuation basis is accepted. A deductible is the part of a loss borne by the insured under the contract. Ask for its exact form and when it applies. A lower premium may come with different limits or a larger contribution from the institution. Do not compare prices alone if inventories and periods differ.

For internal planning, consider where activities could move after damage and what costs would arise. Do not assume that temporary rent, refunded fees or lost income are included in the building policy. If these consequences matter, request a separate explanation of what could be assessed and the conditions that would have to be met.

Review changes before renewal

Check the address, floor areas, activities, rooms and current inventory. Record new purchases and works, together with changes in use. Keep a document calendar and assign someone to maintain it. Do not copy last year's information without checking: a new laboratory or an area rented to another operator may change the necessary questions even if the institution's name stays the same.

For comparison, use a worksheet with three columns: confirmed, unclear and not included. Obtain answers to open questions before signing. The broker can explain options and help organise information; the insurer decides acceptance and handles claims. Management should communicate accurately about the documents in place, without phrases such as all children are completely protected.

Communicate accurately with parents

If the institution announces that it has insurance, base the message on confirmed documents. Explain the actual purpose without disclosing personal data or sensitive information about building security. Do not turn protection for particular assets into a promise of medical assistance or payment for every incident. Before distribution, check the message with the person responsible for the contract and the relevant specialists.

Provide a clear route for questions so that staff do not improvise different conditions from one conversation to the next. If a parent asks about an actual case, distinguish general information from assessment of the incident. Do not request medical details in a public comment. This article does not establish a data-management procedure; it recommends avoiding unnecessary disclosure in communications.

When the contract or activities change, review the messages already in use. Wording that was accurate last year may concern a different period or inventory. Stating the date and purpose helps readers understand its limits. Do not use children's photographs or claims about real experiences to imply protection that is not confirmed in the institution's documents.

Frequently asked questions for administrators

Is there an identical policy for every school?

Do not assume so. Describe the building, activities and property individually. Availability and conditions must be confirmed before drawing conclusions.

Does building insurance pay for every accident involving a child?

No. Property, personal accidents and liability require different assessments. An actual incident calls for checking the facts and documents and, where appropriate, obtaining specialist assistance.

Are computers brought in by teachers included?

Inclusion cannot be assumed. Identify the owner and use, then ask about property belonging to others under the conditions of the actual proposal.

What can I send without providing information about children?

A description of the institution, its premises and activities, an aggregated inventory and the questions to be considered. Personal data are not needed for a general description of the property.
